questions.question: A team is migrating from JSON to Avro for their Kafka messages. Which compatibility type should they set to ensure old consumers using Avro schemas can read data produced with newer Avro schemas?
options: BACKWARD
FORWARD
FULL
NONE
questions.answer: FORWARD
questions.explanation: FORWARD compatibility ensures old consumers (using older schemas) can read data produced with newer schemas. This is critical when consumers might not be updated as quickly as producers during a migration. BACKWARD compatibility is the opposite - it ensures new consumers can read old data.

questions.question: What is the impact of setting unclean.leader.election.enable=true in a Kafka broker?
options: It improves data consistency by preventing out-of-sync replicas from becoming leaders
It prioritizes availability by allowing out-of-sync replicas to become leaders
It increases performance by allowing multiple leaders for the same partition
It enables the Controller to act as a leader for any partition
questions.answer: It prioritizes availability by allowing out-of-sync replicas to become leaders
questions.explanation: Setting unclean.leader.election.enable=true prioritizes availability over consistency. It allows replicas that aren't in the ISR (in-sync replicas) set to become leaders when all current ISR members are unavailable. This can prevent downtime but may cause data loss since out-of-sync replicas might not have all committed data.

questions.question: A producer is sending messages with keys to a topic with 3 partitions. After increasing the topic to 6 partitions, what happens to the key-to-partition mapping?
options: Keys will be distributed to the same partitions as before
All keys will be remapped to potentially different partitions
Only new keys will go to the new partitions; existing keys maintain their original mapping
Keys will be evenly redistributed across all 6 partitions regardless of previous mapping
questions.answer: All keys will be remapped to potentially different partitions
questions.explanation: When partition count changes, the key-to-partition mapping formula (hash(key) % numPartitions) changes. This means all keys will be remapped to potentially different partitions, breaking the key-partition relationship that existed with 3 partitions. This can disrupt applications that rely on key-based ordering or co-partitioning.

questions.question: What is the consequence of setting max.poll.interval.ms too low for a consumer with long record processing times?
options: Records will be processed multiple times
Consumer group rebalances will occur frequently
Records will be skipped if processing takes too long
The consumer will automatically increase the value as needed
questions.answer: Consumer group rebalances will occur frequently
questions.explanation: If max.poll.interval.ms is set too low for a consumer with long processing times, the consumer may fail to call poll() within the specified interval. This causes the broker to consider the consumer failed and trigger a rebalance, reassigning its partitions. Frequent rebalances disrupt processing and impact overall throughput.

questions.question: In a Kafka Streams application, which state store type provides the best read performance but doesn't survive application restarts?
options: Persistent RocksDB store with caching
In-memory state store
Versioned key-value store
TimestampedKeyValueStore
questions.answer: In-memory state store
questions.explanation: In-memory state stores provide the best read performance since they avoid disk I/O, but they don't survive application restarts because data is not persisted. When the application restarts, the state store must be rebuilt from scratch. This contrasts with persistent stores like RocksDB that maintain data on disk and in changelog topics.

questions.question: Which KSQL statement would create a continuously updated table of page view counts per user?
options: CREATE TABLE user_counts AS SELECT userId, COUNT(*) FROM pageviews GROUP BY userId;
CREATE STREAM user_counts AS SELECT userId, COUNT(*) FROM pageviews GROUP BY userId;
CREATE TABLE user_counts AS SELECT userId, COUNT(*) FROM pageviews GROUP BY userId EMIT CHANGES;
CREATE STREAM user_counts AS SELECT userId, COUNT(*) FROM pageviews GROUP BY userId EMIT CHANGES;
questions.answer: CREATE TABLE user_counts AS SELECT userId, COUNT(*) FROM pageviews GROUP BY userId EMIT CHANGES;
questions.explanation: The correct statement is CREATE TABLE with EMIT CHANGES. A TABLE represents an aggregated, continuously updated view (counts per userId), while STREAM would represent each change as a separate event. GROUP BY requires a TABLE for the result, and EMIT CHANGES makes it a continuous query that updates as new data arrives.

questions.question: What determines the maximum possible parallelism for a Kafka Connect sink connector?
options: The number of available Kafka Connect workers
The connector's tasks.max configuration
The number of partitions in the source topic
The CPU cores available on the worker machines
questions.answer: The number of partitions in the source topic
questions.explanation: The maximum parallelism for a sink connector is limited by the number of partitions in the source topic. Each task processes one or more partitions, and a partition cannot be split across multiple tasks. Even if tasks.max is set higher, the connector cannot use more tasks than available partitions.

questions.question: Which command correctly alters the min.insync.replicas setting for an existing topic?
options: kafka-topics.sh --alter --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic my-topic --min-insync-replicas 2
kafka-configs.sh --alter --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --entity-type topics --entity-name my-topic --add-config min.insync.replicas=2
kafka-topics.sh --update --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic my-topic --config min.insync.replicas=2
kafka-admin.sh --alter-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic my-topic --min.insync.replicas 2
questions.answer: kafka-configs.sh --alter --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --entity-type topics --entity-name my-topic --add-config min.insync.replicas=2
questions.explanation: Use kafka-configs.sh to alter configuration for existing topics. The --alter flag indicates a configuration change, --entity-type specifies we're modifying a topic, --entity-name provides the topic name, and --add-config sets the min.insync.replicas parameter to 2. kafka-topics.sh can alter some properties but topic configs are managed through kafka-configs.sh.

questions.question: Which authentication mechanism in Kafka provides integration with enterprise identity management systems via Kerberos?
options: SASL/PLAIN
SASL/SCRAM
SASL/GSSAPI
SSL client certificates
questions.answer: SASL/GSSAPI
questions.explanation: SASL/GSSAPI (Generic Security Services API) is the authentication mechanism that integrates with Kerberos, commonly used in enterprise identity management systems. This allows Kafka to leverage existing Kerberos infrastructure for authenticating clients without maintaining separate credentials within Kafka.

questions.question: Which metric should you monitor to detect if partition leadership is evenly distributed across brokers in a Kafka cluster?
options: UnderReplicatedPartitions
ActiveControllerCount
LeaderCount
OfflinePartitionsCount
questions.answer: LeaderCount
questions.explanation: LeaderCount shows the number of partitions for which a broker is the leader. By comparing this metric across brokers, you can identify imbalances where some brokers have significantly more leader partitions than others, which can lead to uneven load distribution. Significant differences may indicate the need for a leader rebalance.

questions.question: What happens when a KTable-KTable join is performed in Kafka Streams?
options: A new KStream is produced containing all combinations of records with matching keys
A new KTable is produced containing the joined result for each key that exists in both tables
A windowed join result is created that groups records within the same time window
The result depends on which table has more partitions
questions.answer: A new KTable is produced containing the joined result for each key that exists in both tables
questions.explanation: A KTable-KTable join produces a new KTable with joined results for each key present in both input tables. The join result for a key is updated whenever either input table receives an update for that key. This join only includes keys that exist in both tables, similar to an INNER JOIN in SQL.

questions.question: What is the effect of setting enable.idempotence=true on a Kafka producer?
options: It requires the broker to acknowledge all messages
It reduces the chance of message loss at the expense of performance
It prevents duplicate messages caused by producer retries
It guarantees message ordering across partitions
questions.answer: It prevents duplicate messages caused by producer retries
questions.explanation: Setting enable.idempotence=true prevents duplicate messages caused by producer retries. The producer includes a Producer ID and sequence number with each message, allowing the broker to detect and reject duplicates. This provides exactly-once delivery semantics to the broker, ensuring each message is delivered exactly once even when retries occur.

questions.question: What happens if a producer sends a message that exceeds the maximum allowed size for a topic?
options: The producer receives a RecordTooLargeException
The broker truncates the message to fit the maximum size
The message is split into smaller fragments automatically
The message is sent to a special oversized-messages topic
questions.answer: The producer receives a RecordTooLargeException
questions.explanation: When a message exceeds the maximum allowed size (configured by message.max.bytes on the broker or max.message.bytes on the topic), the broker rejects it and the producer receives a RecordTooLargeException. The message is not truncated or automatically split - it's simply rejected. Producers must handle this exception and either reduce the message size or split it manually.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Kafka's CooperativeStickyAssignor?
options: To assign the exact same partitions to consumers as they had previously
To minimize partition movement during rebalances while avoiding stop-the-world pauses
To distribute partitions based on consumer resource capacity
To assign partitions based on geographic proximity to brokers
questions.answer: To minimize partition movement during rebalances while avoiding stop-the-world pauses
questions.explanation: The CooperativeStickyAssignor has two key benefits: 1) it minimizes partition movement during rebalances like the StickyAssignor, and 2) it implements incremental rebalancing, where only affected partitions are reassigned while others continue processing. This avoids the 'stop-the-world' pauses of eager rebalancing strategies, where all consumers pause processing during rebalances.

questions.question: When using Avro with Schema Registry, what happens if a producer tries to send a message with a schema that's incompatible with the existing schema for that topic?
options: The message is sent with a special flag indicating a schema mismatch
The producer receives a SchemaIncompatibleException and the message is not sent
The message is sent with the previous compatible schema version
The message is converted to the existing schema format automatically
questions.answer: The producer receives a SchemaIncompatibleException and the message is not sent
questions.explanation: When a producer tries to register an incompatible schema, the Schema Registry checks it against the compatibility rules (e.g., BACKWARD, FORWARD) and rejects it if incompatible. The producer receives a SerializationException (specifically SchemaIncompatibleException) before any data is sent to Kafka, preventing incompatible data from entering the system.

questions.question: Which is NOT a valid data type in ksqlDB?
options: ARRAY
MAP
CHAR
STRUCT
questions.answer: CHAR
questions.explanation: CHAR is not a valid data type in ksqlDB. ksqlDB supports VARCHAR for string-type data, but not CHAR (fixed-length strings). The other options (ARRAY, MAP, STRUCT) are all valid complex data types in ksqlDB that can be used to represent collections, key-value pairs, and nested structures respectively.

questions.question: What is the significance of the replica.lag.time.max.ms configuration in Kafka?
options: It controls how long a broker will wait for replicas to catch up during shutdown
It determines how often replicas fetch updates from the leader
It specifies how far behind a replica can fall before being removed from the ISR
It sets the maximum time a leader will wait for acknowledgment from followers
questions.answer: It specifies how far behind a replica can fall before being removed from the ISR
questions.explanation: replica.lag.time.max.ms specifies the maximum time a follower can go without fetching from the leader before it's removed from the ISR (In-Sync Replicas). If a replica doesn't request new data within this time, it's considered out-of-sync. This indirectly affects producer acknowledgments when acks=all, as only ISR members must acknowledge for success.

questions.question: In KRaft (Kafka Raft) mode, what is the minimum recommended number of controller nodes for a production environment?
questions.explanation: The minimum recommended number of controller nodes for a production KRaft-based Kafka cluster is 3. This allows the cluster to tolerate the failure of 1 controller node while still maintaining a majority quorum (2 out of 3) for metadata operations. Having only 1 or 2 controller nodes would not provide sufficient fault tolerance for production use.

questions.question: What feature in Kafka Connect helps handle problematic records without failing the entire connector?
options: Exactly-once delivery
Schema validation
Dead Letter Queue
Circuit breaker pattern
questions.answer: Dead Letter Queue
questions.explanation: The Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) feature handles problematic records without failing the entire connector. When errors occur during processing (e.g., schema incompatibilities or transformation failures), these records can be sent to a designated Kafka topic (the DLQ) with error information. This allows the connector to continue processing valid records while providing a mechanism to inspect and potentially fix problematic ones.

questions.question: When migrating a Kafka cluster to use SSL encryption, what is the recommended approach?
options: Switch all traffic to SSL at once by reconfiguring all brokers simultaneously
Start with encrypting client-broker traffic, then inter-broker traffic, and finally close the PLAINTEXT port
Create a new SSL-enabled cluster and migrate data from the old cluster
Enable SSL on a per-topic basis, starting with the most sensitive topics
questions.answer: Start with encrypting client-broker traffic, then inter-broker traffic, and finally close the PLAINTEXT port
questions.explanation: The recommended approach for migrating to SSL is phased: first enable SSL listeners alongside existing PLAINTEXT listeners and migrate clients, then configure inter-broker communication to use SSL, and finally close the PLAINTEXT port. This gradual approach minimizes disruption and provides a fallback path if issues arise during migration.

questions.question: What metric would most effectively help detect consumer lag issues in a Kafka cluster?
options: MessagesInPerSec
BytesOutPerSec
RequestQueueTimeMs
records-lag-max
questions.answer: records-lag-max
questions.explanation: records-lag-max directly measures the maximum lag (in number of messages) between the consumer's current position and the end of the log for any partition. This metric clearly indicates when consumers are falling behind producers, making it the most effective for detecting consumer lag issues. The other metrics may provide general performance insights but don't directly measure consumer lag.

questions.question: Which command is used to reset consumer group offsets in Kafka?
options: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --group mygroup --reset-offsets --to-earliest --execute --topic mytopic
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --alter --group mygroup --reset-offsets --topic mytopic
kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --group mygroup --from-beginning --reset
kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --entity-type groups --entity-name mygroup --alter --add-config offset.reset=earliest
questions.answer: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --group mygroup --reset-offsets --to-earliest --execute --topic mytopic
questions.explanation: The kafka-consumer-groups.sh tool with the --reset-offsets flag is used to reset consumer group offsets. The --to-earliest option resets to the earliest offset, --execute commits the changes (without it, the command runs in dry-run mode), and --topic specifies which topic's offsets to reset. This command is essential for consumer troubleshooting and reprocessing scenarios.

questions.question: What is the advantage of using the SpecificRecord interface with Avro in Kafka instead of GenericRecord?
options: It provides better compression ratios for Avro data
It allows schema-less serialization for flexibility
It generates Java classes with type-safe fields based on the schema
It eliminates the need for Schema Registry integration
questions.answer: It generates Java classes with type-safe fields based on the schema
questions.explanation: SpecificRecord generates Java classes with type-safe fields based on the Avro schema, providing compile-time type checking and more intuitive data access (e.g., customer.getName() instead of customer.get("name")). This reduces runtime errors and improves code readability compared to GenericRecord's map-like interface. Both approaches still require Schema Registry integration for schema management.

questions.question: In a 5-node ZooKeeper ensemble, what is the maximum number of nodes that can fail while still maintaining quorum?
options: 1 node
2 nodes
3 nodes
4 nodes
questions.answer: 2 nodes
questions.explanation: In ZooKeeper, a quorum requires a majority of nodes (more than half) to be operational. With 5 nodes, a majority is 3 nodes (5/2 + 1 = 3). Therefore, the ensemble can tolerate up to 2 node failures while still maintaining a 3-node quorum. If 3 or more nodes fail, the ensemble would have fewer than 3 nodes available and couldn't form a quorum.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a tombstone message in a compacted Kafka topic?
options: To mark a topic as ready for deletion
To indicate that a key should be deleted from the topic
To represent a missing value in stream processing
To signal the end of a transaction
questions.answer: To indicate that a key should be deleted from the topic
questions.explanation: In a compacted topic, a tombstone (a message with a key but null value) indicates that a key should be deleted. When the log cleaner processes a segment with a tombstone, it removes all previous messages with that key. After the delete.retention.ms period, the tombstone itself is removed. This mechanism enables explicit deletion of keys from compacted topics, which is useful for event sourcing patterns.

questions.question: What is the difference between a source connector and a sink connector in Kafka Connect?
options: Source connectors read from Kafka topics, sink connectors write to Kafka topics
Source connectors import data from external systems into Kafka, sink connectors export data from Kafka to external systems
Source connectors are for batch processing, sink connectors are for real-time processing
Source connectors handle structured data, sink connectors handle unstructured data
questions.answer: Source connectors import data from external systems into Kafka, sink connectors export data from Kafka to external systems
questions.explanation: Source connectors import data from external systems (like databases, file systems, or APIs) into Kafka topics. Sink connectors export data from Kafka topics to external systems. The directionality is defined relative to Kafka: source brings data in, sink pushes data out. This fundamental distinction determines connector functionality, configuration, and implementation details.

questions.question: How does Kafka Connect track progress for a source connector that's reading from a database?
options: It uses the kafka consumer group offset mechanism
It maintains a dedicated offset topic to store source offset information
It relies on the database's own transaction log
It requires manual offset tracking in the connector implementation
questions.answer: It maintains a dedicated offset topic to store source offset information
questions.explanation: Kafka Connect tracks source connector progress in a dedicated offset topic (e.g., connect-offsets). For database sources, this typically stores information like table names, primary key values, or timestamp values representing the last ingested row. This automatic offset management is a key feature of Connect, enabling fault tolerance and exactly-once semantics without requiring connector developers to implement their own tracking mechanisms.

questions.question: In Kafka Connect distributed mode, what happens when a worker fails while running several connector tasks?
options: All tasks for that connector stop until the worker is restarted
The tasks are redistributed among remaining workers in the Connect cluster
The tasks continue running on the failed worker with degraded performance
The tasks restart from the beginning of their respective data sources
questions.answer: The tasks are redistributed among remaining workers in the Connect cluster
questions.explanation: When a worker fails in distributed mode, Kafka Connect automatically redistributes its tasks among the remaining workers. This self-healing capability is enabled by storing configurations and offsets in Kafka topics rather than local storage. Task rebalancing works similarly to consumer group rebalancing - the cluster detects the failure and reassigns work to maintain processing continuity with minimal disruption.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Single Message Transforms (SMTs) in Kafka Connect?
options: To convert messages between different serialization formats
To modify individual records as they flow through connectors
To combine multiple small messages into larger batches
To ensure exactly-once processing semantics
questions.answer: To modify individual records as they flow through connectors
questions.explanation: Single Message Transforms (SMTs) allow modifying individual records as they flow through connectors without writing custom code. SMTs perform lightweight record-by-record transformations like field renaming, filtering, value manipulation, or timestamp conversion. They can be chained together and configured declaratively in connector configurations, enabling data customization without developing custom connectors.

questions.question: Which combination of Kafka producer configurations provides at-least-once delivery semantics?
options: acks=0, retries=0
acks=1, retries=0
acks=all, retries>0
enable.idempotence=true, acks=all
questions.answer: acks=all, retries>0
questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery means messages will be delivered, but possibly multiple times if failures occur. Setting acks=all ensures the producer waits for all replicas to acknowledge writes before considering them successful, while retries>0 makes the producer retry failed sends. This combination can cause duplicates on retries (without idempotence) but ensures messages aren't lost, meeting the 'at least once' guarantee. acks=0 would provide at-most-once semantics, while enable.idempotence=true would upgrade to exactly-once semantics.

questions.question: How can a Kafka consumer achieve at-most-once delivery semantics?
options: By setting enable.auto.commit=true and processing records after the auto-commit interval
By setting enable.auto.commit=false and manually committing offsets before processing records
By setting isolation.level=read_committed and enable.auto.commit=true
By using the consumer.commitSync() method after processing each record
questions.answer: By setting enable.auto.commit=false and manually committing offsets before processing records
questions.explanation: At-most-once semantics (process messages at most once) is achieved by committing offsets before processing records. If the consumer crashes after committing but before processing completes, those records won't be reprocessed on restart because the committed offset will be beyond them. This provides protection against duplicate processing at the cost of potential message loss. This pattern requires disabling auto-commit (enable.auto.commit=false) and manually committing offsets before processing.

questions.question: What delivery semantics does Kafka Streams provide when configured with processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2?
options: At-least-once semantics for all stream operations
At-most-once semantics with potential data loss on failure
Exactly-once semantics for all operations within the Kafka cluster
Exactly-once semantics extending to external systems like databases
questions.answer: Exactly-once semantics for all operations within the Kafka cluster
questions.explanation: With processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2, Kafka Streams provides exactly-once semantics for all operations within the Kafka cluster, meaning each input record affects the state and output exactly once, even during failures or rebalances. This is achieved through transactional processing that atomically commits input consumption, state updates, and output production. However, this guarantee only extends to the Kafka ecosystem - when writing to external systems, additional mechanisms are needed to maintain exactly-once semantics end-to-end.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the delivery guarantees of Kafka Connect sink connectors?
options: Kafka Connect always provides exactly-once delivery for all sink connectors
Sink connectors provide at-least-once delivery by default, with exactly-once possible for some connector implementations
Sink connectors only provide at-most-once delivery to prioritize performance
The delivery semantics depend solely on the source topic's configuration, not the connector
questions.answer: Sink connectors provide at-least-once delivery by default, with exactly-once possible for some connector implementations
questions.explanation: Kafka Connect sink connectors provide at-least-once delivery semantics by default, as they store offsets only after successful writes to the destination system. This means a connector might reprocess and rewrite some data if it fails after writing but before storing the offset. Some specific sink connectors can achieve exactly-once semantics if they use idempotent writes or transactions in the destination system, but this capability depends on both connector implementation and destination system features.

questions.question: What is required to achieve true end-to-end exactly-once semantics in a Kafka pipeline that includes producers, streams processing, and external sinks?
options: Enable idempotence for producers, Streams, and consumers
Configure all components with the highest durability settings (acks=all)
Implement idempotent writes or transactional mechanisms in the external sink systems
Use the Kafka transactions API across all components
questions.answer: Implement idempotent writes or transactional mechanisms in the external sink systems
questions.explanation: True end-to-end exactly-once semantics requires idempotent writes or transactional mechanisms in external sink systems. While Kafka can provide exactly-once guarantees within its ecosystem (with producer idempotence, transactional APIs, and Streams exactly_once processing), this guarantee breaks when writing to external systems unless they support idempotent operations or transactions. Examples include databases with upsert capabilities, APIs that support idempotency tokens, or systems with conditional writes that prevent duplicates.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Confluent's Schema Registry integration with Kafka Connect?
options: To enforce schema validation only on the connector configuration
To automatically convert between different data formats like JSON and Avro
To ensure data produced or consumed by connectors conforms to registered schemas
To generate connector configurations based on available schemas
questions.answer: To ensure data produced or consumed by connectors conforms to registered schemas
questions.explanation: Schema Registry integration with Kafka Connect ensures data produced or consumed by connectors conforms to registered schemas. For source connectors, this means data is serialized according to registered schemas before writing to Kafka. For sink connectors, it enables proper deserialization of schema-based formats like Avro. This integration provides data consistency, type safety, and evolution capabilities that are particularly valuable in enterprise environments with strict data governance requirements.

questions.question: What is required for a Kafka producer to achieve exactly-once delivery semantics with idempotence?
options: Set enable.idempotence=true, retries=0, and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=1
Set enable.idempotence=true, while using a transactional.id is optional
Set enable.idempotence=true and use a unique transactional.id for each producer instance
Set enable.idempotence=true, acks=all, and implement a custom deduplication mechanism
questions.answer: Set enable.idempotence=true and use a unique transactional.id for each producer instance
questions.explanation: For exactly-once delivery semantics, a producer needs enable.idempotence=true AND a unique transactional.id. Idempotence alone prevents duplicates from network retries, but for true exactly-once semantics across multiple topic-partition writes, you need the transactional API. The transactional.id enables the broker to distinguish between different producer instances and maintain transaction state across producer restarts.

questions.question: How does a Kafka broker detect and prevent duplicate messages when idempotence is enabled?
options: It uses a bloom filter to track all message IDs ever sent to the topic
It tracks the last 5 message checksums for each producer and rejects duplicates
It maintains sequence numbers for each producer-partition pair and rejects out-of-order duplicates
It requires the client to perform deduplication before sending
questions.answer: It maintains sequence numbers for each producer-partition pair and rejects out-of-order duplicates
questions.explanation: With idempotence enabled, Kafka brokers track sequence numbers for each producer-partition pair. Each producer is assigned a Producer ID (PID), and includes a sequence number with each message. The broker stores the highest sequence number it has received for each PID-partition combination, rejecting messages with already-processed sequence numbers or out-of-order messages. This mechanism detects duplicates from producer retries without requiring the broker to store message contents.

questions.question: What is the impact of setting persistent=false when creating a state store in Kafka Streams?
options: The state store will not use a changelog topic and will lose data on application restart
The state store will use a changelog topic but with a shorter retention period
The state store will be shared across all instances of the application
The state store will not be used for joins or aggregations
questions.answer: The state store will not use a changelog topic and will lose data on application restart
questions.explanation: Setting persistent=false creates an in-memory state store without a changelog topic. This means the state exists only in memory and will be lost on application restart or failure. While this provides faster access by avoiding disk I/O, it sacrifices durability and recoverability. Use in-memory stores only for situations where state reconstruction from input topics is acceptable or where the state is temporary.

questions.question: Which of these operations in Kafka Streams requires a repartition AND maintains state?
options: filter()
flatMap()
map()
groupByKey().count()
questions.answer: groupByKey().count()
questions.explanation: groupByKey().count() requires maintaining state AND can trigger repartitioning. The count() operation maintains a state store to track counts for each key. While groupByKey() itself doesn't require repartitioning (since it groups by the existing key), if any operation before it changed the key, a repartition will occur. The other operations (filter, flatMap, map) are stateless and don't maintain aggregation state, though map() and flatMap() can trigger repartitioning if they change the message key.

questions.question: In Kafka Streams, an application reads from a source topic, filters out some messages, transforms the remaining messages, and writes to an output topic. Which statement is correct about this application?
options: It is stateful because all Kafka Streams applications maintain state
It is stateful because it needs to remember which messages were filtered out
It is stateful because any data transformation requires state
It is stateless because filtering and transformation don't require maintaining state across messages
questions.answer: It is stateless because filtering and transformation don't require maintaining state across messages
questions.explanation: This application is stateless because its operations (filtering and transformation) process each message independently without needing to reference other messages. Stateless operations don't require persistent state stores or changelog topics because they don't need to remember information between messages. Only operations like aggregations, joins, and windowing that need to reference multiple messages are stateful.

questions.question: A banking application uses Kafka to process financial transactions. The system must guarantee that once a transaction is accepted, it will never be lost, even if multiple brokers fail. Which producer configuration provides the strongest durability guarantees?
options: acks=1, min.insync.replicas=1, replication.factor=3
acks=all, min.insync.replicas=1, replication.factor=3
acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, replication.factor=3
acks=all, min.insync.replicas=3, replication.factor=3
questions.answer: acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, replication.factor=3
questions.explanation: The strongest practical durability guarantee comes from acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, replication.factor=3. This ensures writes are acknowledged only when at least 2 replicas (including the leader) have the data, providing protection against data loss if a single broker fails immediately after acknowledging. With replication.factor=3, the system can survive one broker failure while still maintaining the min.insync.replicas=2 requirement. Setting min.insync.replicas=3 would provide stronger guarantees theoretically but would make the system unavailable if any single broker fails.

questions.question: What happens when a producer is configured with acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, replication.factor=3, and all 3 replica brokers are online, but one replica falls significantly behind in replication?
options: Produce requests will be rejected with a NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS exception
Produce requests will succeed because 2 replicas (the leader and one follower) are still in-sync
Produce requests will time out until the lagging replica catches up
The lagging replica will be removed from the ISR, and the leader will continue accepting requests
questions.answer: The lagging replica will be removed from the ISR, and the leader will continue accepting requests
questions.explanation: When a replica falls significantly behind (beyond replica.lag.time.max.ms), it's removed from the In-Sync Replicas (ISR) list. With min.insync.replicas=2 and 2 remaining replicas in the ISR (the leader and one in-sync follower), produce requests will continue to succeed. The leader dynamically manages the ISR based on replica sync status, removing lagging replicas and adding them back when they catch up. This maintains availability while still satisfying the min.insync.replicas requirement.

questions.question: Using the Kafka CLI, which command can be used to display the Kafka version?
options: kafka-topics.sh --version
kafka-server-start.sh --version
kafka-configs.sh --version
kafka-run-class.sh kafka.tools.VersionInfo
questions.answer: kafka-run-class.sh kafka.tools.VersionInfo
questions.explanation: The command kafka-run-class.sh kafka.tools.VersionInfo will display the Kafka version. Unlike many software tools, Kafka doesn't provide a simple --version flag for its standard scripts. Instead, you need to use kafka-run-class.sh to run the VersionInfo tool which displays detailed version information. This is a somewhat unusual approach but is the standard way to check Kafka versions via the command line.

questions.question: Which Kafka CLI command would you use to list all consumer groups in a Kafka cluster?
options: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --all-groups
kafka-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list
kafka-run-class.sh kafka.admin.ConsumerGroupCommand --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list
questions.answer: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list
questions.explanation: To list all consumer groups in a Kafka cluster, use kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list. This command connects to the specified Kafka broker and returns a list of all consumer groups. The --describe flag would provide details about a specific group but requires --group to be specified (or --all-groups in some versions). kafka-groups.sh doesn't exist as a standard Kafka CLI tool. The kafka-run-class version is the older, more verbose way to run the same command.

questions.question: To create a new topic with specific configurations in Kafka, which CLI command is correct?
options: kafka-topics.sh --create --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic my-topic --partitions 3 --replication-factor 2
kafka-topics.sh --create --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic my-topic --num-partitions 3 --replication 2
kafka-admin.sh --create-topic my-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --partitions 3 --replication-factor 2
kafka-run-class.sh kafka.admin.TopicCommand --create --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic my-topic --partitions 3 --replication-factor 2
questions.answer: kafka-topics.sh --create --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic my-topic --partitions 3 --replication-factor 2
questions.explanation: The correct command to create a topic is kafka-topics.sh --create --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic my-topic --partitions 3 --replication-factor 2. This specifies the operation (create), the broker connection, the topic name, the number of partitions, and the replication factor. The parameter is --partitions, not --num-partitions, and --replication-factor, not just --replication. kafka-admin.sh doesn't exist as a standard Kafka CLI tool. While the kafka-run-class version could work in older versions, kafka-topics.sh is the recommended interface.

questions.question: What happens when a producer using Schema Registry encounters a compatibility check failure?
options: The producer automatically falls back to using the previous schema version
The producer throws a SchemaValidationException before sending any data
The message is sent to Kafka with a special flag indicating schema incompatibility
The message is sent to Kafka but the consumer will reject it during deserialization
questions.answer: The producer throws a SchemaValidationException before sending any data
questions.explanation: When a compatibility check fails, the producer throws a SchemaValidationException before sending any data to Kafka. The schema validation occurs during serialization when the producer attempts to register the new schema with Schema Registry. If the schema fails compatibility checks, the producer stops immediately - no data is sent to Kafka, preventing incompatible data from entering the system.

questions.question: In the Confluent Schema Registry, what is a subject?
options: A collection of compatible schema versions for a specific data type
A Kafka topic that contains messages formatted with a specific schema
A user-defined category for organizing schemas with similar structures
A schema validator that enforces rules on record structures
questions.answer: A collection of compatible schema versions for a specific data type
questions.explanation: In Schema Registry, a subject is a collection of compatible schema versions for a specific data type, typically associated with a Kafka topic's key or value. Subjects follow naming conventions like <topic-name>-key or <topic-name>-value. Schema Registry enforces compatibility rules within a subject, ensuring new schemas maintain compatibility with previous versions according to the configured compatibility type.

questions.question: How does Schema Registry handle schema versioning?
options: It uses Git-like versioning with major, minor, and patch numbers
It uses sequential version numbers starting from 1 for each new schema
It generates UUIDs for each schema and stores them in chronological order
It uses hash codes of the schema contents as version identifiers
questions.answer: It uses sequential version numbers starting from 1 for each new schema
questions.explanation: Schema Registry uses simple sequential version numbers for each schema within a subject, starting from 1 for the first registered schema. Each time a new compatible schema is registered under the same subject, its version increments by 1. This approach makes it easy to track schema evolution over time and reference specific versions.

questions.question: What is the difference between Schema Registry's BACKWARD and BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE compatibility modes?
options: BACKWARD checks compatibility only with the most recent version, while BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE checks with all previous versions
BACKWARD only applies to Avro schemas, while BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE works with all schema formats
BACKWARD allows adding optional fields, while BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE doesn't allow any field additions
BACKWARD is for development environments, while BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE is for production use
questions.answer: BACKWARD checks compatibility only with the most recent version, while BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE checks with all previous versions
questions.explanation: BACKWARD compatibility ensures that new consumers using the new schema can read data produced with the most recent previous schema version. BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE extends this by checking compatibility with all previous schema versions, not just the latest one. This stricter mode ensures that consumers using the newest schema can read data written with any previous schema version, providing stronger guarantees for long-lived data.

questions.question: Which REST API endpoint would you use to check compatibility of a new schema against the latest version in a subject?
options: POST /compatibility/subjects/{subject}/versions/latest
GET /subjects/{subject}/versions/latest/compatible
POST /subjects/{subject}/versions/compatible
GET /compatibility/check/{subject}
questions.answer: POST /compatibility/subjects/{subject}/versions/latest
questions.explanation: To check compatibility without registering a schema, use POST /compatibility/subjects/{subject}/versions/latest. This endpoint validates the schema against the latest version in the subject according to the configured compatibility rules, returning whether it would be accepted without actually registering it - useful for testing schema changes before deployment.

questions.question: Which type of join in Kafka Streams requires the input topics to have the same number of partitions and the same partitioning strategy?
options: KStream-to-KStream join only
KTable-to-KTable join only
KStream-to-KTable join only
KStream-to-KStream, KTable-to-KTable, and KStream-to-KTable joins
questions.answer: KStream-to-KStream, KTable-to-KTable, and KStream-to-KTable joins
questions.explanation: KStream-to-KStream, KTable-to-KTable, and KStream-to-KTable joins all require co-partitioned topics, meaning the input topics must have the same number of partitions and use the same partitioning strategy. This ensures that records with the same key are processed on the same task, enabling local joins without data shuffling. Only KStream-to-GlobalKTable joins don't require co-partitioning, as GlobalKTable replicates all data to every instance.

questions.question: Why doesn't a KStream-to-GlobalKTable join require co-partitioning?
options: Because GlobalKTable contains a complete copy of the table data on each instance
Because KStream data is automatically repartitioned during the join operation
Because the join is performed by the Kafka broker, not the Streams application
Because this type of join only supports foreign-key joins, not key-based joins
questions.answer: Because GlobalKTable contains a complete copy of the table data on each instance
questions.explanation: A KStream-to-GlobalKTable join doesn't require co-partitioning because the GlobalKTable contains a complete copy of the table data on each Kafka Streams instance. This means any Streams task can join any KStream record with any GlobalKTable key, regardless of partitioning. This flexibility comes at the cost of increased memory usage, as each instance must hold the entire GlobalKTable dataset.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of converters in Kafka Connect?
options: To convert data between different programming languages
To transform data from one structure to another during ingestion
To translate between Connect's internal data format and serialized Kafka format
To map data types between source and destination systems
questions.answer: To translate between Connect's internal data format and serialized Kafka format
questions.explanation: Converters in Kafka Connect translate between Connect's internal data representation (ConnectRecord with Schema and Value) and the serialized format used with Kafka topics. They handle serialization when writing to Kafka and deserialization when reading from Kafka. Common converters include JsonConverter, AvroConverter with Schema Registry, and StringConverter. Converters operate at the serialization level, not structure transformation or data type mapping.

questions.question: Which configuration in Kafka Connect specifies different converters for a connector's keys and values?
options: key.converter and value.converter
key.serializer and value.serializer
key.format and value.format
key.type and value.type
questions.answer: key.converter and value.converter
questions.explanation: In Kafka Connect, key.converter and value.converter configurations specify different converters for message keys and values. These can be set globally in the worker properties or overridden per connector. For example, you might use StringConverter for keys and JsonConverter for values. Unlike Kafka clients that use serializers/deserializers, Connect uses converters which handle both serialization and deserialization within the Connect framework.

questions.question: What is a Serde in Kafka Streams, and how is it related to Serializers and Deserializers?
options: Serde is a configuration property that controls how data is processed in the Streams API
Serde is a wrapper that contains both a Serializer and a Deserializer for a specific data type
Serde is a special type of stream processor that handles data format conversions
Serde is a storage format optimized for stateful operations in Kafka Streams
questions.answer: Serde is a wrapper that contains both a Serializer and a Deserializer for a specific data type
questions.explanation: In Kafka Streams, a Serde (Serializer/Deserializer) is a wrapper that contains both a Serializer and a Deserializer for a specific data type. It provides a convenient way to configure both serialization and deserialization with a single object. The Kafka Streams API requires Serdes for specifying how to serialize/deserialize keys and values when reading from or writing to Kafka topics. Common implementations include Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long(), and custom Serdes for application-specific types.

questions.question: Which method in the Kafka Serializer interface is responsible for converting a Java object to bytes?
options: convert(String topic, T data)
serialize(String topic, T data)
toBytes(String topic, T data)
transform(String topic, T data)
questions.answer: serialize(String topic, T data)
questions.explanation: The serialize(String topic, T data) method in the Kafka Serializer interface is responsible for converting a Java object to bytes. This method takes the topic name and the data object as parameters and returns a byte array. The topic parameter allows implementing topic-specific serialization if needed. The Deserializer interface has a complementary deserialize(String topic, byte[] data) method for the reverse transformation.

questions.question: When operating ksqlDB in headless mode, where does ksqlDB store metadata, and what information is stored in the corresponding storage?
options: In ZooKeeper, storing query definitions and state
In local files on each ksqlDB server, storing query execution plans
In the Kafka cluster, storing command and command topics with DDL statements
In an external metadata database, storing schemas and queries
questions.answer: In the Kafka cluster, storing command and command topics with DDL statements
questions.explanation: In headless mode, ksqlDB stores metadata in internal Kafka topics within the Kafka cluster itself. Specifically, it uses a command topic (default: _confluent-ksql-{serviceId}_command_topic) to store all DDL statements (CREATE, DROP), CSAS/CTAS queries, and TERMINATE statements. This approach ensures durability and enables multiple ksqlDB servers to share the same metadata and maintain consistent state, allowing for distributed operations and fault tolerance.

questions.question: Which of the following is a stateless operation in Kafka Streams?
options: aggregate()
count()
join()
filter()
questions.answer: filter()
questions.explanation: Filter() is a stateless operation in Kafka Streams as it processes each record independently without needing to store any state between records. It simply evaluates a predicate function on each input record and passes or drops it accordingly. The other options are stateful: aggregate() maintains aggregation state, count() keeps running counts, and join() requires matching records from multiple streams/tables with state stores.

questions.question: What is the key difference between stateful and stateless operations in Kafka Streams?
options: Stateful operations are faster than stateless operations
Stateful operations require local state stores, while stateless operations don't
Stateful operations are only available in the DSL, not the Processor API
Stateful operations support exactly-once semantics, while stateless don't
questions.answer: Stateful operations require local state stores, while stateless operations don't
questions.explanation: The key difference is that stateful operations require local state stores to maintain data across multiple records, while stateless operations don't. Stateful operations (like aggregations, joins, windowing) need to remember previous records to compute their results, using persistent state stores backed by changelog topics for fault tolerance. Stateless operations (filter, map, flatMap) process records independently without maintaining state, making them simpler but less powerful for complex processing.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a changelog topic in Kafka Streams state stores?
options: To log application errors for debugging purposes
To store the complete processing history of the application
To back up the state store for fault tolerance and recovery
To capture metadata about the stream processing topology
questions.answer: To back up the state store for fault tolerance and recovery
questions.explanation: Changelog topics back up state stores for fault tolerance and recovery in Kafka Streams. When a stateful operation uses a state store, changes are logged to a changelog topic in addition to the local store. If a Streams instance fails, its tasks can be reassigned and rebuild their state stores by replaying the changelog, ensuring recovery without data loss. Changelogs enable the exactly-once processing semantics Kafka Streams provides.

questions.question: How does Kafka Streams handle state stores during rebalancing?
options: State stores are lost and must be rebuilt from scratch after rebalancing
State stores are automatically transferred to the new instance via direct network transfer
State stores are rebuilt by replaying the changelog topic on the new instance
State stores are saved in ZooKeeper and restored on the new instance
questions.answer: State stores are rebuilt by replaying the changelog topic on the new instance
questions.explanation: During rebalancing, Kafka Streams rebuilds state stores by replaying their changelog topics on the new instances that take ownership of the partitions. When tasks are reassigned due to scaling or failure, the new instance reads from the changelog topic to reconstruct the exact state before the rebalance. This approach ensures consistent state without requiring direct transfer between instances, leveraging Kafka's built-in persistence and replication.

questions.question: What is the Schema Registry's global compatibility setting?
options: A default compatibility mode that applies to all subjects unless overridden
A compatibility check that ensures schemas work across multiple Kafka clusters
A mode that enforces the same schema across all topics in the Kafka cluster
A configuration that determines whether schemas are stored globally or per-topic
questions.answer: A default compatibility mode that applies to all subjects unless overridden
questions.explanation: The global compatibility setting in Schema Registry is a default compatibility mode (e.g., BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL) that applies to all subjects unless specifically overridden at the subject level. When new schemas are registered, they're checked against this global setting if no subject-specific setting exists. You can configure different compatibility modes for specific subjects while letting others use the global default.

questions.question: What happens when you request the latest schema for a subject from Schema Registry?
options: You get the most recently registered schema, regardless of compatibility
You get the schema with the highest version number
You get the schema that is most compatible with your client version
You get the schema that is most widely used by producers
questions.answer: You get the schema with the highest version number
questions.explanation: When requesting the latest schema for a subject, Schema Registry returns the schema with the highest version number. Schema Registry tracks versions sequentially, so the highest version number represents the most recently registered compatible schema. This behavior allows clients to always retrieve the most up-to-date schema definition, which is particularly useful for consumers that need to deserialize data produced with various schema versions.

questions.question: For a KTable-to-KTable join in Kafka Streams, when is the join result updated?
options: Only when both KTables receive updates with matching keys
Whenever either KTable receives an update to a key that exists in both tables
At regular intervals defined by a windowing configuration
Only when explicitly triggered by an application-defined function
questions.answer: Whenever either KTable receives an update to a key that exists in both tables
questions.explanation: In a KTable-to-KTable join, the join result is updated whenever either KTable receives an update to a key that exists in both tables. Since KTables represent the current state for each key, any change to either table for a shared key triggers a join computation and produces a new result. This behavior enables maintaining a continuously updated joined view that reflects the latest state of both tables.

questions.question: Which of these statements about the JsonSerializer in Kafka is correct?
options: It automatically registers schemas with Schema Registry
It requires a Jackson ObjectMapper to be configured
It provides full schema evolution support like the AvroSerializer
It automatically handles type information like Java generics
questions.answer: It requires a Jackson ObjectMapper to be configured
questions.explanation: The JsonSerializer in Kafka requires a Jackson ObjectMapper to be configured for customizing JSON serialization. Unlike AvroSerializer, it doesn't integrate with Schema Registry by default or provide the same level of schema evolution support. JsonSerializer also can't automatically preserve complete type information like Java generics, which can cause issues with complex types unless explicitly handled.

questions.question: A team needs to implement a custom serializer/deserializer for complex objects in their Kafka application. Which methods must they implement in a custom Serializer<T> class?
options: serialize(String topic, T data) only
serialize(String topic, T data) and deserialize(String topic, byte[] data)
serialize(String topic, T data), configure(Map<String, ?> configs, boolean isKey), and close()
serialize(String topic, Headers headers, T data) and toBytes(T data)
questions.answer: serialize(String topic, T data), configure(Map<String, ?> configs, boolean isKey), and close()
questions.explanation: A custom Serializer<T> class must implement three methods: serialize(String topic, T data), configure(Map<String, ?> configs, boolean isKey), and close(). The serialize method is the core method that converts the object to a byte array. The configure method initializes the serializer with configuration properties and indicates whether it's for keys or values. The close method handles any cleanup. The deserialize method is part of the Deserializer interface, not the Serializer interface. The serializer and deserializer are separate classes in Kafka, unlike some other systems that combine them. The other option with Headers and toBytes contains method signatures that don't exist in Kafka's Serializer interface.

questions.question: When using Avro with Schema Registry in a Kafka application, how are schemas validated?
options: Schemas are validated against previously registered schemas when a producer attempts to register a new schema
Schemas are validated by the broker before it accepts messages with the schema
Schemas are validated when a consumer attempts to deserialize a message
Schemas are not validated; Schema Registry only stores them for reference
questions.answer: Schemas are validated against previously registered schemas when a producer attempts to register a new schema
questions.explanation: When using Avro with Schema Registry, schemas are validated against previously registered schemas when a producer attempts to register a new schema. The Schema Registry enforces compatibility rules (based on the configured compatibility type like BACKWARD, FORWARD, or FULL) by checking if the new schema is compatible with existing schemas for the same subject. This validation happens before the schema is registered and before any data is actually produced. The broker doesn't validate schemas directly - it just receives serialized data. Consumers typically don't trigger validation; they simply request the schema from the registry to deserialize messages. Schema Registry isn't just a passive storage system; it actively enforces compatibility rules to prevent breaking changes.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the __transaction_state internal topic in Kafka?
options: It stores consumer group offset information
It manages the transactional state for transactions across multiple topics and partitions
It tracks which messages have been processed in exactly-once delivery scenarios
It contains metadata about topic configurations
questions.answer: It manages the transactional state for transactions across multiple topics and partitions
questions.explanation: The __transaction_state internal topic manages the transactional state for transactions across multiple topics and partitions. This topic is used by Kafka's transaction coordinator to maintain information about ongoing transactions, including their status (started, preparing to commit, committed, or aborted). It enables Kafka's transactional capability, which allows producers to send messages to multiple topics and partitions atomically, ensuring that either all messages in a transaction are committed or none are. The __consumer_offsets topic (not __transaction_state) stores consumer group offsets. Exactly-once delivery uses transactional IDs and producer IDs but doesn't have a dedicated tracking topic. Topic configuration metadata is stored in ZooKeeper or in KRaft metadata, not in a dedicated internal topic.

questions.question: When migrating a Kafka cluster, what special consideration must be given to internal topics like __consumer_offsets?
options: They must be manually recreated on the new cluster, as they cannot be migrated
They should not be migrated as the new cluster will automatically recreate them
They should be migrated using a different tool than regular application topics
They should be migrated like regular topics, but with careful attention to partition count and replication factor
questions.answer: They should be migrated like regular topics, but with careful attention to partition count and replication factor
questions.explanation: When migrating a Kafka cluster, internal topics like __consumer_offsets should be migrated like regular topics, but with careful attention to preserving their partition count and replication factor. These internal topics contain critical metadata, and migrating them correctly ensures that consumer groups maintain their offset positions and other internal state. Simply recreating them on the new cluster would lose all current offset information, potentially causing consumers to reprocess data or skip messages. No special tool is needed for internal topics versus regular topics - standard migration tools like MirrorMaker can handle them. However, it's crucial to ensure that these topics are included in the migration plan and that their configuration (particularly partition count) matches the source cluster to maintain the same hashing behavior for keys.

questions.question: A Kafka producer is sending sensor reading messages where occasional message loss is acceptable, but low latency is critical. Which configuration is most appropriate?
options: acks=all, retries=3, batch.size=16384, linger.ms=0
acks=1, retries=1, batch.size=16384, linger.ms=5
acks=0, retries=0, batch.size=16384, linger.ms=0
acks=1, retries=0, compression.type=snappy, batch.size=32768
questions.answer: acks=0, retries=0, batch.size=16384, linger.ms=0
questions.explanation: For a scenario where occasional message loss is acceptable but low latency is critical, the most appropriate configuration is acks=0, retries=0, batch.size=16384, linger.ms=0. Setting acks=0 means the producer doesn't wait for any acknowledgment from the broker, which minimizes latency at the cost of potential message loss if the broker fails. Setting retries=0 ensures that failed sends aren't retried, which could otherwise introduce delays. Using batch.size=16384 (a modest value) and linger.ms=0 (no artificial delay) ensures messages are sent immediately without waiting to batch. While compression might improve throughput, it adds CPU overhead and potentially increases latency. The other options prioritize reliability over latency with their acks and retries settings, which doesn't match the specified requirements.

questions.question: What is the effect of setting enable.idempotence=true on a Kafka producer?
options: It only prevents duplicate messages if acks=all is also set
It automatically adjusts retries, acks, and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection to ensure exactly-once delivery
It ensures exactly-once processing for consumers reading the produced messages
It prevents the producer from sending multiple messages with the same key
questions.answer: It automatically adjusts retries, acks, and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection to ensure exactly-once delivery
questions.explanation: Setting enable.idempotence=true automatically adjusts several configurations to ensure exactly-once delivery semantics: retries is set to Integer.MAX_VALUE, acks is set to 'all', and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection is capped at 5. These settings work together to prevent duplicates while maintaining message order. When idempotence is enabled, the producer includes a Producer ID and sequence numbers with each message, allowing the broker to detect and reject duplicates. This ensures exactly-once delivery to the Kafka log, not exactly-once processing by consumers (which requires additional mechanisms). Option A is incorrect because the producer automatically sets acks=all. Option C is incorrect because idempotence doesn't affect consumer processing semantics. Option D is incorrect because idempotence doesn't prevent multiple messages with the same key - it prevents the same message from being written multiple times.

questions.question: A Kafka consumer application performs complex processing on each message, and occasionally takes longer than the default settings allow. Which configuration change would prevent consumer group rebalances due to processing delays?
options: Increase session.timeout.ms
Decrease heartbeat.interval.ms
Increase max.poll.interval.ms
Set enable.auto.commit=false
questions.answer: Increase max.poll.interval.ms
questions.explanation: When a consumer performs complex processing that takes longer than default settings allow, increasing max.poll.interval.ms is the appropriate configuration change to prevent rebalances due to processing delays. This parameter controls the maximum time between consecutive poll() calls before the consumer is considered failed. When processing takes too long, the consumer might exceed this interval, causing it to be removed from the group and triggering a rebalance. Increasing session.timeout.ms would prevent rebalances due to missed heartbeats, but that's a different issue than slow processing. Decreasing heartbeat.interval.ms would send heartbeats more frequently but wouldn't help if poll() isn't called. Setting enable.auto.commit=false changes how offsets are committed but doesn't affect the max.poll.interval.ms timeout.

questions.question: What partition assignment strategy in Kafka minimizes the reassignment of partitions during consumer group rebalances?
options: RangeAssignor
RoundRobinAssignor
StickyAssignor
DefaultAssignor
questions.answer: StickyAssignor
questions.explanation: The StickyAssignor partition assignment strategy minimizes the reassignment of partitions during consumer group rebalances. Unlike RangeAssignor and RoundRobinAssignor, which completely reassign partitions without considering the previous assignment, StickyAssignor tries to maintain the existing partition-to-consumer assignments as much as possible during rebalances. It only reassigns partitions when necessary (e.g., when consumers join or leave the group), and it attempts to balance the number of partitions per consumer. This 'stickiness' reduces the impact of rebalances by minimizing partition movement, which helps maintain local consumer state and reduces the need to reload data. There is no DefaultAssignor - the default strategy in recent Kafka versions is actually the RangeAssignor, though this may vary by client version.

questions.question: Which Kafka broker configuration controls how long the broker will wait for all followers to acknowledge a write before responding to the producer when acks=all?
options: replica.lag.time.max.ms
request.timeout.ms
min.insync.replicas
replica.fetch.wait.max.ms
questions.answer: replica.lag.time.max.ms
questions.explanation: The replica.lag.time.max.ms configuration controls how long the broker will wait for all followers to acknowledge a write before responding to the producer when acks=all. This parameter defines the maximum time a follower can lag behind the leader before it's removed from the ISR (In-Sync Replicas) list. When a producer uses acks=all, the leader waits for acknowledgments from all ISRs before responding. If a follower doesn't acknowledge within replica.lag.time.max.ms, it's removed from the ISR, and the leader proceeds with the remaining ISRs. This parameter thus indirectly controls the maximum wait time for acknowledgments. The min.insync.replicas setting defines the minimum number of replicas that must acknowledge a write, not the wait time. request.timeout.ms is a client-side setting, not a broker configuration. replica.fetch.wait.max.ms doesn't exist as a standard Kafka configuration.

questions.question: A Kafka broker is configured with log.retention.hours=168 and log.retention.bytes=1073741824. How will these settings affect log retention?
options: Logs will be retained for exactly 168 hours, with the oldest logs deleted first
Logs will be retained indefinitely unless the total size exceeds 1073741824 bytes
Logs will be retained for 168 hours AND until the total size exceeds 1073741824 bytes
Logs will be retained for 168 hours OR until the total size exceeds 1073741824 bytes, whichever comes first
questions.answer: Logs will be retained for 168 hours OR until the total size exceeds 1073741824 bytes, whichever comes first
questions.explanation: When both time-based (log.retention.hours=168, or 7 days) and size-based (log.retention.bytes=1073741824, or 1GB) retention policies are configured, Kafka applies them as an OR condition. This means logs will be retained for 168 hours OR until the total size exceeds 1073741824 bytes, whichever comes first. If the log exceeds 1GB before 7 days, older segments will be deleted to maintain the size limit. If the log doesn't exceed 1GB within 7 days, segments older than 7 days will be deleted regardless of the total size. This approach ensures that both time and space constraints are respected independently, providing more flexible resource management. The policies are applied at the log segment level, not individual messages.

questions.question: A team adds a new required field to an Avro schema with BACKWARD compatibility enabled. What will happen?
options: The new schema will be accepted because adding fields is always backward compatible
The new schema will be rejected because adding required fields breaks backward compatibility
The new schema will be accepted only if all existing data already contains this field
The new schema will be accepted but existing data will be automatically converted to include the new field
questions.answer: The new schema will be rejected because adding required fields breaks backward compatibility
questions.explanation: With BACKWARD compatibility enabled, adding a new required field (a field without a default value) will be rejected because it breaks backward compatibility. Backward compatibility ensures that new schema versions can read data written with old schema versions. When a required field is added, new consumers using the new schema would expect this field to be present in all records, but old records written with the previous schema won't have this field, causing deserialization failures. For a field addition to be backward compatible, the field must have a default value so that new readers can populate the field with the default when reading old data. Adding a field with a default value would be acceptable with BACKWARD compatibility, but adding a required field is not.

questions.question: Which schema evolution change is allowed under BOTH BACKWARD and FORWARD compatibility modes?
options: Changing a field's type from int to long
Removing a required field
Adding a field with a default value
Renaming a field without using aliases
questions.answer: Adding a field with a default value
questions.explanation: Adding a field with a default value is allowed under BOTH BACKWARD and FORWARD compatibility modes. For BACKWARD compatibility, when new readers using the new schema read old data that doesn't contain the field, they can use the default value. For FORWARD compatibility, when old readers using the old schema read new data that contains the extra field, they simply ignore it since they don't know about it. The other options break at least one compatibility mode: Changing a field's type from int to long breaks both BACKWARD and FORWARD compatibility due to potential data misinterpretation. Removing a required field breaks BACKWARD compatibility because new readers would expect the field to be absent while old data would have it. Renaming a field without aliases breaks both compatibility modes because readers would be looking for a different field name than what's in the data.

questions.question: Which of the following operations in Kafka Streams does NOT trigger a repartitioning?
options: stream.selectKey((k, v) -> v.getUserId())
stream.groupBy((k, v) -> v.getCategory())
table.groupBy((k, v) -> KeyValue.pair(v.getRegion(), v))
stream.filter(v -> v.getAmount() > 1000)
questions.answer: stream.filter(v -> v.getAmount() > 1000)
questions.explanation: The filter() operation does NOT trigger a repartitioning in Kafka Streams. Filter is a stateless operation that simply evaluates each record against a predicate and passes or drops it without changing the record's key or the required partition distribution. The other operations all cause repartitioning because they change the message key: selectKey() explicitly changes the key used for the stream, groupBy() groups records by a different key than their original key, and table.groupBy() creates a new grouping with a different key. Any operation that changes the key requires a repartitioning to ensure that all records with the same key are routed to the same partition for correct processing, particularly for operations like joins and aggregations that rely on co-location of related records.

questions.question: What's the difference between KTable.toStream() and KTable.toStream(Named.as("name"))?
options: The second version creates a named stream for better visualization in tools like Topology Viewer
The second version creates a named changelog topic instead of using an auto-generated name
The first version converts the KTable to a KStream, while the second creates a persistent QueryableStateStore
There is no functional difference; the second version just adds a name for logging and metrics
questions.answer: There is no functional difference; the second version just adds a name for logging and metrics
questions.explanation: There is no functional difference between KTable.toStream() and KTable.toStream(Named.as("name")); the second version just adds a name for the operation that's used in logging and metrics. Both methods convert a KTable (which represents a changelog stream with the current value for each key) to a KStream (which represents a stream of key-value pairs). The Named.as() parameter doesn't create a named topic or state store, nor does it change the runtime behavior. It simply assigns a name to that step in the topology, which appears in logs, metrics, and visualization tools. This can be helpful for debugging and monitoring but doesn't alter the functional behavior of the application or how data flows through the topology.

questions.question: Which feature of Kafka Connect is specifically designed to handle errors during message transformation or processing without failing the entire connector?
options: Exactly-once delivery semantics
Offset management
Dead Letter Queue
Schema evolution
questions.answer: Dead Letter Queue
questions.explanation: The Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) feature in Kafka Connect is specifically designed to handle errors during message transformation or processing without failing the entire connector. When a connector encounters problematic records (due to schema incompatibilities, transformation errors, or connector-specific issues), these records can be sent to a designated Kafka topic (the DLQ) along with error information, rather than failing the entire pipeline. This allows the connector to continue processing valid records while providing a mechanism to inspect and potentially fix the problematic ones. To use this feature, connectors can be configured with settings like errors.tolerance=all and errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name to specify the DLQ topic. The other options are important Kafka Connect features but don't directly address error handling: exactly-once semantics ensure records are processed exactly once, offset management tracks progress, and schema evolution handles changing data structures.

questions.question: What is the difference between standalone and distributed modes in Kafka Connect?
options: Standalone mode runs on a single worker, while distributed mode spreads tasks across a cluster of workers
Standalone mode is for development only, while distributed mode is for production
Standalone mode connects to a single Kafka cluster, while distributed mode connects to multiple clusters
Standalone mode supports only a subset of connectors, while distributed mode supports all connectors
questions.answer: Standalone mode runs on a single worker, while distributed mode spreads tasks across a cluster of workers
questions.explanation: The key difference between standalone and distributed modes in Kafka Connect is that standalone mode runs on a single worker, while distributed mode spreads tasks across a cluster of workers. In standalone mode, all connector and task configurations are defined in local configuration files, and all tasks run on the same worker node. In distributed mode, configurations are submitted via the REST API and stored in Kafka topics, allowing tasks to be distributed across multiple workers for scalability and fault tolerance. Standalone mode is not limited to development environments and can be used in production for simpler deployments. Both modes can connect to the same Kafka clusters and support the same set of connectors. The choice between modes depends primarily on scalability, fault tolerance, and operational requirements rather than connector compatibility or environment type.

questions.question: Which of the following primitive types is NOT supported in KSQL?
options: VARCHAR
LONG
BYTES
CHAR
questions.answer: CHAR
questions.explanation: KSQL supports several primitive data types including VARCHAR (variable-length string), LONG (64-bit signed integer), and BYTES (variable-length byte array). However, it does NOT support CHAR (fixed-length string) as a data type. Instead, it only supports VARCHAR for string-type data. The supported primitive types in KSQL include: BOOLEAN, INTEGER/INT, BIGINT, DOUBLE, STRING/VARCHAR, BYTES, DECIMAL, and DATE/TIME types (DATE, TIME, TIMESTAMP).
