CHAR is typically found in traditional relational databases but is not part of the KSQL type system.

questions.question: Which of the following functions can be used for invocation of KSQLDB lambda expressions?
options: TRANSFORM and REDUCE
MAP and FILTER
APPLY and FOREACH
LAMBDA and EXECUTE
questions.answer: TRANSFORM and REDUCE
questions.explanation: In KSQLDB, lambda expressions (which allow you to pass code as arguments to functions) can be invoked using the TRANSFORM and REDUCE functions. TRANSFORM applies a lambda expression to each element in an array and returns an array with the results. REDUCE applies a lambda expression to reduce an array to a single value by iteratively combining elements. Functions like MAP and FILTER are common in other stream processing systems but aren't used for lambdas in KSQLDB. APPLY, FOREACH, LAMBDA, and EXECUTE are not built-in KSQLDB functions for lambda invocation.

questions.question: A team has a production Kafka topic with Avro-serialized messages. They want to delete a field from their schema that is no longer needed. Several applications still use the old schema to consume data. Which compatibility mode would allow this change while ensuring existing consumers continue to work?
options: FORWARD
BACKWARD
FULL
NONE
questions.answer: FORWARD
questions.explanation: FORWARD compatibility ensures that old consumers (using the old schema) can read data produced with the new schema. Deleting a field is forward compatible because old consumers expecting that field will still be able to read new data - the field will just be populated with the default value if specified, or null for union types with null. BACKWARD compatibility wouldn't be sufficient here because it ensures new consumers can read old data, which doesn't address existing consumers using the old schema. FULL requires both FORWARD and BACKWARD compatibility. NONE would allow any change but removes all compatibility guarantees, which would be risky for production systems.

questions.question: A development team wants to evolve an Avro schema by changing the type of a field from 'int' to 'long'. Which compatibility setting would permit this change?
options: BACKWARD
FORWARD
FULL
None of the above
questions.answer: None of the above
questions.explanation: Changing a field's type from 'int' to 'long' is not allowed under any of the standard compatibility modes (BACKWARD, FORWARD, or FULL). This is because type changes are generally not compatible in either direction: New consumers expecting a 'long' might misinterpret old 'int' values (breaking backward compatibility), and old consumers expecting an 'int' might misinterpret new 'long' values (breaking forward compatibility). The only way to make this change would be to set compatibility to NONE, which turns off compatibility checking, or to use a more complex schema evolution approach such as adding a new field with the long type while maintaining the old int field during a transition period.

questions.question: An organization uses Schema Registry with BACKWARD compatibility and wants to merge two separate Avro schemas into a single schema to streamline development. The merged schema needs to be compatible with data written using both original schemas. How should they approach this?
options: Make all fields in the merged schema optional with default values
Use schema unions to combine both original schemas exactly as they are
Set compatibility to NONE during the merge, then revert to BACKWARD after completion
The merge is not possible while maintaining BACKWARD compatibility
questions.answer: Make all fields in the merged schema optional with default values
questions.explanation: To merge two Avro schemas while maintaining BACKWARD compatibility, making all fields in the merged schema optional with default values is the correct approach. With BACKWARD compatibility, newer schema versions must be able to read data written with older schemas. By making all fields optional (using unions with null) and providing default values, the merged schema can properly handle data written with either of the original schemas, even when fields from one original schema are missing in records written with the other original schema. Schema unions wouldn't be BACKWARD compatible because the writer schema must be a valid subtype of the reader schema. Setting compatibility to NONE is risky and unnecessary in this case.

options: Yes, because enums are compatible with strings in Avro schema evolution
Yes, but only if all existing string values match one of the enum symbols
No, changing from string to enum breaks both FORWARD and BACKWARD compatibility
No, but it would be compatible under BACKWARD compatibility mode
questions.answer: No, changing from string to enum breaks both FORWARD and BACKWARD compatibility
questions.explanation: Changing a field from a string type to an enum type breaks both FORWARD and BACKWARD compatibility in Avro. This is because: 1) New readers (expecting an enum) cannot correctly interpret old data (containing arbitrary strings), breaking BACKWARD compatibility, and 2) Old readers (expecting strings) cannot correctly interpret new data (containing enum values), breaking FORWARD compatibility. Since FULL compatibility requires both FORWARD and BACKWARD compatibility, this change would be rejected. The change would not be compatible under any of the standard compatibility modes unless all existing string values were already exactly matching the enum symbols, which would be rare in practice.

questions.question: A Kafka producer needs to ensure maximum throughput while still guaranteeing that messages are successfully written to the cluster. Which configuration combination best achieves this?
options: acks=all, batch.size=16384, linger.ms=0, compression.type=none
acks=1, batch.size=65536, linger.ms=10, compression.type=lz4
acks=0, batch.size=131072, linger.ms=100, compression.type=snappy
acks=all, batch.size=131072, linger.ms=5, compression.type=zstd
questions.answer: acks=1, batch.size=65536, linger.ms=10, compression.type=lz4
questions.explanation: For maximum throughput while still guaranteeing successful message delivery, the optimal configuration is: acks=1, batch.size=65536, linger.ms=10, compression.type=lz4. This combination provides a good balance: acks=1 ensures the leader replica acknowledges writes (offering reasonable durability without waiting for follower replicas); a large batch.size allows efficient batching; linger.ms=10 allows batches to fill while adding minimal latency; and lz4 compression provides excellent compression/speed ratio. acks=all would provide stronger durability but reduce throughput. acks=0 offers no guarantee of successful delivery. linger.ms=0 prevents batching optimization. Compression.type=none misses an opportunity for throughput gains, while zstd is more CPU-intensive than lz4.

questions.question: What is the effect of setting max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5 and retries=3 on a producer without enabling idempotence?
options: Increased throughput with guaranteed message order
Increased throughput with possible message reordering
Reduced throughput with guaranteed message order
Reduced throughput with possible message reordering
questions.answer: Increased throughput with possible message reordering
questions.explanation: Setting max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5 allows the producer to have up to 5 requests in flight at once, which increases throughput by enabling parallelism. However, when combined with retries=3 without enabling idempotence (enable.idempotence=true), this configuration can lead to message reordering. If an earlier request fails and is retried while later requests succeed, the retried message might end up being written after messages that were sent later, breaking the original order. This is a classic throughput vs. ordering trade-off. Setting max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=1 would maintain order but reduce throughput, while enabling idempotence would maintain both order and throughput.

questions.question: A Kafka producer application needs to handle messages that exceed the broker's maximum message size limit. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Increase the broker's message.max.bytes configuration to accommodate larger messages
Enable compression on the producer to reduce message size
Split large messages into chunks at the application level with correlation IDs
Set max.request.size on the producer to match the broker's limit and catch exceptions
questions.answer: Split large messages into chunks at the application level with correlation IDs
questions.explanation: The most appropriate approach for handling messages that exceed the broker's maximum size limit is to split them into chunks at the application level with correlation IDs. This allows reconstruction of the complete message on the consumer side while working within Kafka's message size constraints. Increasing message.max.bytes on the broker could work but might impact cluster performance and would require administrative access. Compression helps but may not be sufficient for very large messages. Setting max.request.size equal to the broker limit doesn't solve the problem - it just ensures consistent rejection behavior. Implementing a chunking protocol at the application level provides the most robust and scalable solution.

questions.question: What is the impact of setting isolation.level=read_committed on a Kafka consumer?
options: The consumer will only read records that were produced as part of committed transactions or outside of transactions
The consumer will wait for all messages to be committed to all replicas before reading them
The consumer will only read records after committing its own offsets
The consumer will require the broker to have unclean.leader.election.enable=false
questions.answer: The consumer will only read records that were produced as part of committed transactions or outside of transactions
questions.explanation: Setting isolation.level=read_committed means the consumer will only read records that were either produced outside of a transaction (non-transactional messages) or were produced as part of a transaction that was successfully committed. Records that are part of ongoing transactions or aborted transactions will not be visible to the consumer. This provides transaction isolation guarantees, ensuring that consumers only see consistent, committed transactional data. The default isolation.level=read_uncommitted allows consumers to read all messages regardless of transaction state. This setting is independent of how consumers commit their own offsets or broker replication configurations.

questions.question: A Kafka consumer application processes streaming data and occasionally needs to reprocess earlier data. Which combination of consumer configurations would best support this requirement?
options: enable.auto.commit=true, auto.offset.reset=earliest
enable.auto.commit=false, auto.offset.reset=earliest
enable.auto.commit=true, auto.offset.reset=latest
enable.auto.commit=false, auto.offset.reset=none
questions.answer: enable.auto.commit=false, auto.offset.reset=earliest
questions.explanation: For an application that occasionally needs to reprocess earlier data, setting enable.auto.commit=false and auto.offset.reset=earliest is optimal. With enable.auto.commit=false, the application takes control of when offsets are committed, allowing it to explicitly reset positions when reprocessing is needed (via seek()). Setting auto.offset.reset=earliest ensures that when the consumer starts without a committed offset (such as after resetting), it will start from the beginning of the topic. The combination of manual offset management and earliest reset behavior gives the application maximum flexibility to reprocess data when needed while still making normal forward progress during standard operation.

questions.question: In a high-throughput Kafka consumer application, which of these configurations has the LEAST impact on consumer performance?
options: fetch.max.bytes
max.poll.records
heartbeat.interval.ms
fetch.min.bytes
questions.answer: heartbeat.interval.ms
questions.explanation: The heartbeat.interval.ms configuration has the least impact on consumer performance in a high-throughput scenario. This parameter controls how frequently the consumer sends heartbeats to the group coordinator to indicate it's still alive, but it doesn't directly affect the data consumption path. The other options all directly impact throughput: fetch.max.bytes limits how much data can be fetched in a single request; max.poll.records limits how many records are returned in a single poll() call; and fetch.min.bytes can cause the broker to wait until enough data is available before responding. While heartbeat frequency is important for group membership, it operates on a separate channel from data consumption and doesn't typically become a bottleneck.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of configuring multiple consumers with the same group.id?
options: To increase the availability of the consumer application through redundant processing
To distribute the processing load by allocating different partitions to each consumer
To ensure exactly-once processing semantics for messages
To replicate consumer offset information across multiple instances
questions.answer: To distribute the processing load by allocating different partitions to each consumer
questions.explanation: The primary purpose of configuring multiple consumers with the same group.id is to distribute the processing load by allocating different partitions to each consumer. Kafka's consumer group mechanism ensures that each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer within the group, allowing for parallel processing of data across partitions. This is Kafka's fundamental scaling mechanism for consumption: adding more consumers to a group increases processing capacity up to the number of partitions in the topic. It doesn't provide redundant processing (each message is processed by only one consumer in the group), doesn't ensure exactly-once semantics (that's handled by other mechanisms), and doesn't replicate offset information (offsets are stored centrally in the __consumer_offsets topic).

questions.question: A Kafka cluster needs to maximize throughput for producers while ensuring no data loss in case of a single broker failure. Which broker configuration best achieves this goal?
options: default.replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=1, unclean.leader.election.enable=true
default.replication.factor=2, min.insync.replicas=1, unclean.leader.election.enable=false
default.replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=2, unclean.leader.election.enable=false
default.replication.factor=1, min.insync.replicas=1, unclean.leader.election.enable=false
questions.answer: default.replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=2, unclean.leader.election.enable=false
questions.explanation: To maximize throughput while ensuring no data loss with a single broker failure, the optimal configuration is: default.replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=2, unclean.leader.election.enable=false. With 3 replicas, the cluster can tolerate one broker failure while still maintaining 2 copies of the data. Setting min.insync.replicas=2 ensures that writes are acknowledged only when at least 2 replicas (including the leader) have the data, providing protection against data loss if a single broker fails immediately after acknowledging. Setting unclean.leader.election.enable=false prevents out-of-sync replicas from becoming leaders, which could cause data loss. This configuration balances durability and availability while supporting high throughput.

questions.question: Which Kafka broker configuration parameter controls the number of threads used for processing requests after they've been accepted from the network?
options: num.network.threads
num.io.threads
request.handler.threads
num.replica.fetchers
questions.answer: num.io.threads
questions.explanation: The num.io.threads configuration parameter controls the number of threads used for processing requests after they've been accepted from the network. These threads handle the actual request processing logic and any associated disk I/O operations. The num.network.threads parameter controls the number of threads used for accepting connections and performing network I/O, not for request processing. The request.handler.threads parameter doesn't exist in Kafka broker configuration. The num.replica.fetchers parameter controls the number of threads used for fetching data from leader replicas, which is a specific function and not related to general request processing.

questions.question: What is the function of the log.segment.bytes parameter in Kafka broker configuration?
options: Controls the maximum size of messages that can be received by the broker
Sets the maximum size of a single log segment file before a new one is created
Limits the total size of all log segments for a topic before deletion
Defines the buffer size used for replicating data between brokers
questions.answer: Sets the maximum size of a single log segment file before a new one is created
questions.explanation: The log.segment.bytes parameter sets the maximum size of a single log segment file before a new one is created. In Kafka, each partition's log is divided into segments for easier management. When a segment reaches the size specified by log.segment.bytes, it is closed and a new one is created. This parameter affects how frequently segments are rolled and consequently how often they become eligible for deletion through log retention policies. Smaller segments mean more frequent rollovers and potentially more granular retention, but also more files to manage. This parameter doesn't control message size (that's message.max.bytes), limit total log size (that's log.retention.bytes), or affect replication buffer sizes.

options: When the Schema object is created with new Schema.Parser().parse(...)
When the GenericRecord is created with new GenericData.Record(schema)
When the ProducerRecord is created with new ProducerRecord<>(...)
When producer.send(record) is called
questions.answer: When producer.send(record) is called
questions.explanation: The Avro schema is registered with Schema Registry when producer.send(record) is called, not earlier in the process. The KafkaAvroSerializer (specified as the value.serializer) handles schema registration automatically during the serialization process, which occurs as part of the send() operation. Prior steps like creating the Schema object, creating the GenericRecord, or creating the ProducerRecord don't interact with the Schema Registry - they only create local objects in memory. It's only when the producer needs to actually serialize the record for sending that it uses the KafkaAvroSerializer, which checks if the schema is already registered, and if not, registers it with the Schema Registry before serializing the data.

options: The producer will throw an immediate exception when send() is called
The producer will retry sending the message 3 times with 1-second backoff, then throw an exception
The producer will retry indefinitely until close() is called, then throw an exception
The producer will write to a local buffer and attempt to deliver when the broker is available
questions.answer: The producer will retry sending the message 3 times with 1-second backoff, then throw an exception
questions.explanation: With the given configuration (retries=3, retry.backoff.ms=1000), the producer will retry sending the message 3 times with a 1-second backoff between attempts when the broker is unavailable. Since the send() call is used without a callback and the results are not checked, the exception won't be thrown immediately at the send() line. However, when producer.close() is called, it will wait for all in-flight requests to complete (including retries). At this point, if the message couldn't be sent after all retry attempts, an exception will be thrown. The producer doesn't retry indefinitely (it's limited by the retries setting) and doesn't maintain a persistent local buffer that survives closure for future delivery.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the difference between a KStream and a KTable in Kafka Streams?
options: KStream represents a log of changes where each record is independent, while KTable represents the latest state for each key
KStream can only be created from topics, while KTable can be derived from computation results
KStream supports stateless operations, while KTable only supports stateful operations
KStream is limited to primitive data types, while KTable supports complex objects
questions.answer: KStream represents a log of changes where each record is independent, while KTable represents the latest state for each key
questions.explanation: The fundamental difference between KStream and KTable is that a KStream represents a log of changes where each record is treated as an independent event, while a KTable represents the latest state for each key (like a continuously updated lookup table). With a KStream, every record is processed individually regardless of its key. With a KTable, each record is treated as an update to the current value for that key, so only the latest value per key is maintained. This difference affects how operations like aggregations and joins work on each abstraction. Both KStream and KTable can be created from topics or derived from operations, both support stateless and stateful operations, and both work with the same data types.

questions.question:
Analyze the following ksqlDB query:

```sql
CREATE TABLE page_view_counts AS
  SELECT pageId,
         COUNT(*) AS view_count
  FROM page_views
  WINDOW TUMBLING (SIZE 1 HOUR)
  GROUP BY pageId
  EMIT CHANGES;
```

What will this query produce?
options: A table showing the all-time count of views for each page
A stream of page view events enriched with running counts
A table with windowed keys containing pageId and window boundaries, with counts for each 1-hour window
A stream that emits updated page counts every hour
questions.answer: A table with windowed keys containing pageId and window boundaries, with counts for each 1-hour window
questions.explanation: This ksqlDB query creates a windowed table (CREATE TABLE with WINDOW clause) that counts page views grouped by pageId in 1-hour tumbling windows. The result is a table where the key consists of both the pageId and window boundaries (start and end time), and the value contains the view_count for each window. As new page_views records arrive, they're assigned to the appropriate 1-hour window based on their timestamp, and the count for that pageId and window is updated. It's not an all-time count (option A) because of the windowing, not a stream of individual events (option B) because it's an aggregate table, and not a periodic emission (option D) because records are updated continuously as specified by EMIT CHANGES.

questions.question:
Consider the following Kafka Streams code:

```java
KStream<String, Order> orders = ...
KTable<String, Customer> customers = ...

KStream<String, EnrichedOrder> joined = orders.join(
    customers,
    (order, customer) -> new EnrichedOrder(order, customer)
);
```

What condition must be true for this join to work correctly?
options: The orders stream and customers table must use the same serialization format
The orders stream and customers table must have the same number of partitions
The message key in the orders stream must match the key in the customers table
The customers table must be entirely loaded into memory before joining
questions.answer: The message key in the orders stream must match the key in the customers table
questions.explanation: For a join between a KStream (orders) and a KTable (customers) in Kafka Streams, the message key in the orders stream must match the key in the customers table for records to be joined. This join is essentially a lookup operation where each order is enriched with customer information based on matching keys. Additionally, the topics must be co-partitioned (same number of partitions and same partitioning strategy) so that records with the same key are in the same partition, but this is an underlying requirement not explicitly stated in the code. The serialization format is handled by serdes configurations and doesn't affect the join logic itself. The customers table doesn't need to be entirely loaded into memory; Kafka Streams manages state stores efficiently.

questions.question: When configuring a JDBC Source Connector to incrementally load data from a relational database table, which of the following properties is essential for tracking the position in the table?
options: connection.url
mode
incrementing.column.name
batch.size
questions.answer: incrementing.column.name
questions.explanation: When configuring a JDBC Source Connector for incremental loading, the incrementing.column.name property is essential for tracking position in the table. This property specifies an autoincrementing column (like an ID) that the connector uses to identify new rows since the last poll. Each time the connector runs, it retrieves rows where this column's value is greater than the last seen value, allowing it to capture only new or updated data. While connection.url is required for connecting to the database, mode would specify the overall loading approach (e.g., bulk, incrementing, timestamp), and batch.size controls how many records are processed at once, none of these track the actual position in the table like incrementing.column.name does.

questions.question: In Kafka Connect, what determines the maximum parallelism that can be achieved by a sink connector?
options: The tasks.max configuration of the connector
The number of Kafka Connect worker nodes in the cluster
The number of partitions in the source topic
The number of available CPU cores on the worker nodes
questions.answer: The number of partitions in the source topic
questions.explanation: In Kafka Connect, the maximum parallelism that can be achieved by a sink connector is determined by the number of partitions in the source topic. Each task processes a subset of partitions, and a partition cannot be split across multiple tasks. Therefore, even if tasks.max is set to a high value, the connector cannot use more tasks than there are partitions in the topic. The tasks.max configuration only sets an upper limit on the number of tasks, and the connector may use fewer tasks based on the available partitions. While the number of worker nodes and CPU cores affects the cluster's overall capacity, they don't directly limit a single connector's parallelism like the partition count does.

questions.question: A team needs to implement a custom serializer/deserializer for complex objects in their Kafka application. Which methods must they implement in a custom Serializer<T> class?
options: serialize(String topic, T data) only
serialize(String topic, T data) and deserialize(String topic, byte[] data)
serialize(String topic, T data), configure(Map<String, ?> configs, boolean isKey), and close()
serialize(String topic, Headers headers, T data) and toBytes(T data)
questions.answer: serialize(String topic, T data), configure(Map<String, ?> configs, boolean isKey), and close()
questions.explanation: A custom Serializer<T> class must implement three methods: serialize(String topic, T data), configure(Map<String, ?> configs, boolean isKey), and close(). The serialize method is the core method that converts the object to a byte array. The configure method initial
